# Global Bishop Discs in Almost Complex Stein Domains

## Overview

The study of Bishop discs constitutes an important area within complex geometry, with significant implications for understanding the structure of pseudoconvex domains. In this work, researchers examine the existence of global Bishop discs within strictly pseudoconvex Stein domains, focusing specifically on the setting of almost complex manifolds of complex dimension 2. This investigation extends classical results from the integrable case into the more general and challenging framework of non-integrable almost complex structures.

## Background and Motivation

Bishop discs—named after Errett Bishop, who pioneered their study—are pseudoholomorphic discs whose boundaries lie on prescribed submanifolds, typically totally real submanifolds or the boundaries of domains. These objects serve as fundamental tools for probing the geometry of complex and almost complex manifolds. In the classical integrable setting, the theory is well developed, and Bishop discs have proven essential for questions concerning envelopes of holomorphy, polynomial convexity, and the fine structure of pseudoconvex boundaries.

The transition to almost complex manifolds introduces substantial difficulties. When the almost complex structure fails to be integrable, many of the standard techniques from several complex variables no longer apply directly. The absence of local holomorphic coordinates, in particular, forces a reliance on more analytic and geometric methods, including the theory of pseudoholomorphic curves developed in the context of symplectic geometry.

## The Central Problem

The researchers address the question of whether *global* Bishop discs exist within strictly pseudoconvex Stein domains equipped with an almost complex structure. The distinction between local and global existence is crucial: while local Bishop discs can often be constructed by perturbative arguments near a point, establishing the existence of discs that extend globally throughout the domain requires controlling the pseudoholomorphic curves over a much larger region. Strict pseudoconvexity provides essential geometric control, ensuring favorable properties for the boundary behavior of these discs.

## Main Result

The principal contribution of this work is a proof that such global Bishop discs do in fact exist within the specified class of domains. Working in complex dimension 2, the authors establish the existence result through careful analysis of the relevant pseudoholomorphic curve equations, exploiting the strict pseudoconvexity of the Stein domain to guarantee the necessary compactness and boundary regularity.

## Significance

This result advances the understanding of complex geometric structures in non-integrable almost complex settings. By demonstrating that global Bishop discs persist even in the absence of integrability, the work broadens the scope of classical complex-analytic techniques and provides new tools for studying the geometry of almost complex manifolds. These findings contribute to the ongoing effort to develop a coherent theory of pseudoconvexity and holomorphic-type objects in the almost complex category, with potential applications to problems in symplectic geometry and the analysis of pseudoholomorphic curves.

# Opening Statement

## Existence Results in Almost Complex Geometry of Dimension Two

The study of almost complex manifolds occupies a central position at the intersection of differential geometry, symplectic topology, and complex analysis. An almost complex structure on a smooth manifold $M$ of real dimension $2n$ is an endomorphism $J \colon TM \to TM$ of the tangent bundle satisfying $J^2 = -\mathrm{Id}$, equipping each tangent space with the structure of a complex vector space. While every almost complex manifold shares certain formal features with genuine complex manifolds, the fundamental question of *integrability*—whether $J$ arises from an honest holomorphic atlas—remains delicate and is governed by the vanishing of the Nijenhuis tensor, as established by the celebrated theorem of Newlander and Nirenberg.

The case of complex dimension two, corresponding to real dimension four, is distinguished by a wealth of special structure absent in higher dimensions. Here the interplay between the almost complex structure, the conformal geometry of the base, and the algebraic topology of four-manifolds gives rise to phenomena with no analogue elsewhere. The Hodge star operator acts as an involution on the space of two-forms, inducing the self-dual/anti-self-dual decomposition that underlies gauge theory and the modern classification of four-manifolds. It is precisely in this dimension that Seiberg–Witten invariants, Gromov's theory of pseudoholomorphic curves, and the Enriques–Kodaira classification converge, providing a rich toolkit for both the construction and the obstruction of geometric structures.

In this paper, we address the existence of almost complex structures satisfying prescribed geometric and analytic constraints on four-dimensional manifolds. Motivated by classical questions concerning the compatibility of almost complex structures with symplectic or metric data, we develop techniques that combine local analytic constructions with global topological input. Our principal results establish the existence of such structures under natural hypotheses, and we clarify the extent to which the obstructions encountered are essential rather than merely technical.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. After fixing notation and recalling the requisite background in Section 2, we formulate our main theorems in Section 3. Sections 4 and 5 are devoted to the construction and the verification of the required properties, respectively, and we conclude with a discussion of applications and open problems.
